title: Terraform 1000-Foot View
subtitle: A simple first mental model for Terraform

nodes.label: Terraform
nodes.definition: Terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool used to define and manage cloud or platform infrastructure through configuration files.
nodes.whyItMatters: It helps teams avoid one-off manual setup and makes infrastructure changes more repeatable and reviewable.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform lets teams describe infrastructure as code, review changes with a plan, and apply approved changes in a controlled way.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not describe Terraform as just a script runner. It is a desired-state infrastructure tool.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform is used to define infrastructure in code, compare that desired state with what exists, and then apply controlled changes.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as Code
nodes.definition: Infrastructure as Code means infrastructure is described in files instead of being created only by clicking through a console.
nodes.whyItMatters: Version-controlled infrastructure is easier to review, repeat, share, and audit.
nodes.safeSentence: Infrastructure as Code makes cloud resources more repeatable and less dependent on manual console work.
nodes.commonTrap: IaC does not automatically make infrastructure safe. Teams still need review, state control, and good process.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Infrastructure as Code lets teams manage resources like networks, storage, compute, and permissions through reviewed configuration files.

nodes.label: Desired State
nodes.definition: Desired state is what the Terraform configuration says should exist.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform uses desired state to decide what needs to be created, changed, or removed.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform starts from the desired state and figures out what changes are needed to reach it.
nodes.commonTrap: Desired state is not the same as current reality. Real infrastructure can drift.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform compares the desired configuration with what it knows about the real environment, then proposes changes.

nodes.label: Providers
nodes.definition: Providers are Terraform plugins that know how to talk to platforms such as AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, or monitoring tools.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform itself needs providers to understand how to create and manage real platform resources.
nodes.safeSentence: A provider is the bridge between Terraform and the platform being managed.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse a provider with a resource. The provider connects; the resource is the managed object.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Providers let Terraform interact with external platforms like AWS by calling their APIs.

nodes.label: Resources
nodes.definition: Resources are the infrastructure objects Terraform manages, such as an S3 bucket, EC2 instance, IAM role, VPC, log group, dashboard, or alert.
nodes.whyItMatters: Resources are the real things Terraform creates, changes, or removes.
nodes.safeSentence: A resource is the infrastructure object Terraform manages.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not think a resource is only a server. It can be many kinds of cloud or platform objects.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Resources are the actual objects described in Terraform configuration and tracked through state.

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.definition: Plan previews what Terraform intends to create, update, or destroy before changes are applied.
nodes.whyItMatters: Plan is the safety checkpoint where humans review the blast radius.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform plan is the preview step before changing real infrastructure.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not skip plan review, especially in shared or production environments.
nodes.interviewAnswer: The plan step is important because it shows what Terraform will change before anything is applied.

externalLinks.label: Open Core Workflow Deep Study Page

nodes.label: Apply
nodes.definition: Apply performs the approved Terraform changes against the target platform.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is where the reviewed plan becomes real infrastructure.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform apply should happen only after the plan has been reviewed.
nodes.commonTrap: Running apply casually can change or destroy real infrastructure.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Apply is the execution step where Terraform carries out the reviewed infrastructure changes.

nodes.label: State
nodes.definition: State is Terraform's memory of the infrastructure it manages and how the code maps to real resources.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without state, Terraform would not know what it already created or manages.
nodes.safeSentence: State is critical because it connects Terraform configuration to real infrastructure.
nodes.commonTrap: State can be sensitive and dangerous if deleted, corrupted, exposed, or edited carelessly.
nodes.interviewAnswer: State is one of the most important Terraform concepts because it tracks managed infrastructure and supports change comparison.

nodes.label: Drift
nodes.definition: Drift happens when real infrastructure changes outside Terraform and no longer matches the expected configuration or state.
nodes.whyItMatters: Drift can cause confusion, unexpected plans, and operational risk.
nodes.safeSentence: Drift means the real environment no longer matches what Terraform expects.
nodes.commonTrap: Manual console changes can create drift if they bypass the Terraform workflow.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Drift is when infrastructure is changed outside Terraform, causing a mismatch between code, state, and reality.

nodes.label: Team Safety
nodes.definition: Team safety means using Terraform with review, version control, remote state, locking, access control, and disciplined apply workflows.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform can change important infrastructure, so teams need guardrails.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform is powerful, so teams need safe workflows around review, state, and change control.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat Terraform as a solo local tool when a team or production environment is involved.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Safe Terraform use is about plan review, controlled apply, protected state, locking, and version-controlled infrastructure changes.

nodes.label: IaC: Why Terraform Exists
nodes.definition: Open the pre-intro map that explains the IaC landscape and why Terraform exists.
nodes.whyItMatters: This lets Sean move backward from the Terraform operating model to the broader IaC landscape and competing tools.
nodes.safeSentence: Before going deeper into Terraform, it helps to understand the IaC landscape and why Terraform became popular.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not mix this navigation bubble with core Terraform concepts. It is a map doorway, not a Terraform building block.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform is one tool in the larger Infrastructure as Code landscape, alongside tools such as CloudFormation, Ansible, Pulumi, and OpenTofu.
